questions.q: Who created Solidity in 2014, and what other blockchain did they go on to create?
options: Gavin Wood, who also created Polkadot
Vitalik Buterin, who also created Bitcoin
Satoshi Nakamoto, who also created Ethereum Classic
Nobody named in this lesson
questions.explain: Gavin Wood, a co-founder of Ethereum itself, created Solidity in 2014 and later founded the Polkadot blockchain.

questions.q: What real alternative to Solidity uses Python-like syntax?
options: Vyper
Yul
Fe
questions.explain: Vyper is described as "Pythonic" — if you already know Python, its syntax will look familiar, though the languages aren't identical.

questions.q: What does compiling a Solidity file actually do?
options: Converts human-readable Solidity code into machine-readable bytecode the EVM can execute
Deletes the source code permanently
Automatically deploys the contract to the blockchain
Converts bytecode back into Solidity
questions.explain: Compiling transforms your readable `.sol` source code into low-level bytecode — the format the EVM actually understands and executes.

questions.q: Per this lesson, why does checking your wallet balance cost zero gas while swapping tokens costs gas?
options: Checking a balance is a readable function that doesn't change state; swapping is a writable function that does
Checking a balance always costs more gas than swapping
Gas cost has nothing to do with reading or writing state
Both actions cost the exact same amount of gas
questions.explain: Readable functions don't modify the blockchain's state and are free; writable functions change state (like an actual token swap) and require gas.

questions.q: What is Yul, as described in this lesson?
options: An intermediate language commonly used inside Solidity to optimize gas costs, at the expense of readability
A replacement for the EVM itself
A JavaScript framework unrelated to Ethereum
The official name for Solidity's compiler
questions.explain: Yul is an intermediate language used to hand-optimize gas costs in specific parts of a Solidity program — powerful but much less readable than Solidity itself.
